text.title: GraphQL API Design Worked Examples
text.summary: Two end-to-end worked examples applying the methodology — a multi-client dashboard and a payment mutation with userErrors and @auth. Output matches the schema in content/02-output-contract.xml.

section.title: Trace
section.paragraph: Need: dashboard with org/user/orders, web+mobile clients. → New GraphQL service. → Design SDL with Relay pagination on orders. → Add OrganizationLoader and OrdersByUserLoader, per-request in context. → permission_classes=[IsOrgMember] on every org-scoped resolver. → QueryDepthLimiter(10) + QueryComplexityExtension(200).

section.title: Second example — payment mutation with userErrors and @auth
section.paragraph: The payments aggregate ships createPayment(input: CreatePaymentInput!): CreatePaymentPayload @auth(scope: PAYMENTS_WRITE). CreatePaymentPayload carries { payment: Payment, userErrors: [UserError!]! }, and UserError carries { field, message, code } — so "insufficient balance" arrives as a userError, not as a transport error. Payment.author resolves to User through an opaque global ID (gid://app/User/abc) rather than the Postgres integer. Paginated lists use PaymentConnection. The schema diff gate is green and the @auth coverage report shows 100% on mutations and sensitive fields. The legacy Boolean-returning createPayment is migrated by field deprecation with removal targeted at v2.0.

section.title: Decision path applied
section.paragraph: The decision tree in content/06-decision-tree.xml routed both inputs to the recommended action: the shape gates checked mutation payloads, userErrors, directive-declared auth, Connection naming and opaque IDs in that order before reaching the approve leaf. Each rule referenced by the conclusions is listed in content/01-core-rules.xml.
